title: Why Do You Go Blind 15,000 Times a Day? 👁️
description:
Why do we blink, and why doesn't the world go dark when we do? Each blink spreads a fresh tear film over your eye, while your brain quiets its visual system so you never see the blackout.

topic: Why do you blink thousands of times a day?
script: You go blind fifteen thousand times every day. Why can't you tell? It's called blinking. Each blink lasts about a tenth of a second. The clear front of your eye has no blood vessels, so it relies on a film of tears instead. That film has three parts: mucus, water, and oil. Every blink wipes on a fresh coat, like a tiny windshield wiper, and sweeps dust toward your eye's drain. So why doesn't the world go black? Scientists scanned people's brains during blinks, and found parts of the visual system go quiet, right as your eyelid comes down. Your brain deletes the blackout, before you can ever see it. Altogether, your eyes are shut for about half an hour every day. So how many seconds can you go without blinking? Tell me your record.
key_facts: About 15 blinks a minute, commonly cited as around 15,000 a day
Tear film spreads with each blink: mucus, water, oil; cornea has no direct blood supply
Brain activity in visual areas is suppressed during blinks (Bristow 2005; Golan 2016)
Roughly half an hour a day of eyes shut, by commonly cited estimates
